Greg Hollis, Total Rewards. Before we post the Sacramento roles, I need to know one thing: where do the pay bands come from?
They were built from the Austin data and then adjusted. The adjustment has been reviewed by finance, but not by you yet.
Then let me slow you down. In California the range must be posted in the ad, so whatever we write is public on day one.
Understood. And in Texas?
No posting requirement in Texas. But engineers talk to each other, so assume every number will be compared, whatever the law says.
That is exactly my worry about pay equity. If two people do the same job in two states, how do you explain the gap?
With cost of living, and only cost of living. If location does not explain the difference, it should not be there. We had our own bands audited last year for that reason.
Then I would like ours to be audited too, before anything is posted. I would rather we explain the gap than have the engineers discover it.

Every new client shows me their base salaries first, and I understand why. It is the number on the offer letter. But it is not what people compare once they are inside. In the US, the health plan can be worth twenty or thirty percent of the salary, and the employer match on retirement is the first thing an experienced engineer asks about. So when I am asked, are we paying enough, my first answer is always another question: enough of what? The second thing I tell clients is about transparency. In California, Washington and a growing list of places, the range has to be published. That means your pay bands are not a private document any more. They are a public promise. If you cannot explain a gap in one sentence, you should assume it will be explained for you, and not kindly.

Two years ago one of our best engineers came to me with an offer from a competitor. Fifteen percent more. We matched it within a day, and I was proud of how fast we moved. Eight months later he left anyway, and this time he did not come to me first. When I looked back, the money had never been the real problem. He had been asking for a different role for a year, and the request had been parked in every review. The counteroffer told him we would pay to keep him, but not that we would change anything. What I do now is simple. When somebody brings me an offer, I ask what they would need to stay if the money were the same. Sometimes the answer is money. More often than not, it is something that should have been fixed a year earlier.
